pragmatic

/prag-MAT-ik/ - the stress falls on MAT · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Pragmatic means guided by what actually works in practice rather than by theories or ideals.

The pragmatic captain abandoned the record attempt at the first ice warning; a finished voyage, she said, beats a famous one.

Example

When the water grant finally arrived, half the committee wanted the solar pumping array — silent, modern, gleaming in the brochures. Ines, the committee's pragmatic chair, priced the replacement parts, counted the certified technicians within a hundred miles (two), and asked what happened in the rainy season. Then she ordered simple hand pumps the village blacksmith could strip and fix by lunchtime. Ten years on, every one of them still pours.

Pragmatic is the word for Ines because her test for every option was the same: will it work here, for us, and keep working? Not the most inspiring choice, not the most modern — the one that pours in year ten. Notice the word passes no judgment on ideals themselves; it just refuses to let them outrank results. The brochure was beautiful. The blacksmith was real.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

practical: Practical is the everyday twin — focused on what can be done with the tools at hand. Pragmatic adds a strategist's edge: it's practical as a policy, deliberately ranking what works above what would be ideal.

realistic: Realistic is about seeing: a realistic view takes the situation as it actually is. Pragmatic is about doing — the word for choices that act on that clear view and let results decide.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

idealistic: steering by principles and dreams, whatever the odds

utopian: designing for a perfect world that practice can't deliver

Where it sits · how far results are allowed to outrank ideals

sensible → pragmatic → expedient

sensible vs. pragmatic: Sensible is milder than pragmatic: a sensible choice merely avoids obvious folly, while a pragmatic one goes further and deliberately trades the ideal answer for the one that will work.

expedient vs. pragmatic: Expedient goes further than pragmatic — the pragmatic mayor bends an ideal to get results, but the expedient one drops the principle entirely if that speeds the outcome.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — pragma: a deed, a thing done (Greek prassein, "to do")

Suffix — -tic: relating to; adjective-forming

Put it together: Pragma- (Greek pragma, "a deed, a thing done") + -tic (relating to) = concerned with deeds. Greek prassein, "to do," powers a whole family of get-it-done words — practice, practitioner, practical — and pragmatic keeps the faith: every idea judged by what it does rather than what it promises.

Use the root in a new word: pragmatism: Voters credited the mayor's pragmatism when the potholes were finally filled ahead of the ribbon-cuttings.

Root Check

Word Choice

level-headed / faintly admiring

Pragmatic is praise with its sleeves rolled up: it credits someone with ranking results above ideals, and only lightly hints at the ideals set aside. This unit's judicious honors the quality of the weighing; pragmatic honors the outcome-first tiebreak. Push results-worship one notch further — principle dropped for speed — and the honest word turns to expedient.
